So yeah... it's definitely messing up my relationships at home, but the fact that the guys at the station are losing faith in me? That's what's really terrifying me right now. Oh, man, yeah. Absolutely. It's funny you ask about that age, because I was actually just talking to my mom about this a few weeks ago, right after that awful meeting with my captain. I was venting to her about how I can't seem to just stand still, and she just kind of laughed and sighed at the same time. 

She says I was exactly like this back in grade school, too. I mean, probably even more obvious back then because I didn't have any kind of adult filter or way to hide it. She told me it was just a constant, exhausting struggle from the moment I hit first or second grade. I was always, always the kid who was out of his seat. Like, the teacher would be up at the chalkboard explaining fractions or whatever, and I'd be up at the pencil sharpener for the fifth time, or wandering over to look at the class pet, or just standing by my desk because sitting in that hard little plastic chair felt like absolute torture. My body just rejected it. 

And it wasn't just the moving around, either. I was constantly blurting out answers. If the teacher asked a question and I knew it, I couldn't raise my hand and wait to be called on. I just couldn't physically hold it in. The answer would just shoot out of my mouth before I even realized I was talking. I didn't mean to be disrespectful or disrupt the class, it just... bypassed my brain entirely. 

And the homework... oh man, my poor mom. It was a total nightmare. I was constantly losing my assignments. She would sit down with me at the kitchen table, we'd spend an hour doing a math worksheet, I'd physically put it into my folder, and somehow by the time I got to school the next morning, it was just gone. Vanished. Sucked into a black hole in my backpack. So, of course, the teachers were always sending notes home. My mom kept a whole file of them, I swear, and it was always the exact same story. They'd write, "He's a bright boy, he grasps the concepts, he's smart enough to do the work, but he just won't sit still," or "He needs to learn to stay in his seat and stop interrupting." 

It used to drive my parents crazy because they knew I wasn't stupid, you know? Like, they knew I was bright enough to get straight A's, but I was getting C's and D's on my report card for "citizenship" or "conduct" just because I couldn't sit quietly at a desk for six hours a day. So yeah, this definitely isn't some new thing that just popped up as an adult. It's been my whole life, really. Just this motor running inside me that won't ever shut off, ever since I was a little kid.

It's like this intense, physical pressure building up in my chest and my legs, almost like a coiled spring or a pressure valve that's stuck closed. I just kept bouncing my knee, shifting my weight around, taking my boots off and putting them back on, tapping my pen... I guess I was clicking my pen for like twenty minutes straight without even realizing it, because Martinez—he drives Engine 7, great guy, but he has zero patience—he actually reached over and grabbed the pen right out of my hand and told me to knock it off. \n\nSo, yeah, I wouldn't say I feel anxious, necessarily. I'm not sitting there stressing about my bills or anything. It's just this unbearable, physical need to stand up and do literally anything else. If I'm forced to just sit there and I can't move, I just feel like I'm gonna explode out of my own skin.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel this intense need to move or do something when you're not at work, like when you're at home or out with friends?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. It’s definitely not just a firehouse thing. Honestly, it might actually be worse at home because there’s no structured chaos to hide behind, you know? Like, even on my days off, which you’d think would be my time to just decompress and catch my breath... I always tell them I'm just going to the kitchen for a glass of water, but then I wander off. Half the time I end up out in the garage. I'll be out there checking my tools, reorganizing my socket wrenches by size, or making sure the lithium batteries on my power drills are fully charged. \n\nAnd then my wife will come out to the garage like an hour later, just standing there in the doorway looking at me like, 'What are you doing? It’s like, if the activity is quiet, I have to fill the silence by talking, or moving, or fixing something. No, actually... no, they never did. It's just... general, chaotic movement, I guess. Whatever is handy, whatever gets me out of the chair, whatever keeps my hands busy. I just want to make sure I'm being clear about that, because it's definitely not some kind of organized compulsion. It's just my body needing to do *something* to stop feeling like it's going to crawl out of its own skin.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience this intense need to move or restlessness when you were a child, before you turned 12?\n\nPatient: Oh, man, yeah. Absolutely. It's funny you ask about that age, because I was actually just talking to my mom about this a few weeks ago, right after that awful meeting with my captain. I was venting to her about how I can't seem to just stand still, and she just kind of laughed and sighed at the same time. \n\nShe says I was exactly like this back in grade school, too. I mean, probably even more obvious back then because I didn't have any kind of adult filter or way to hide it. She told me it was just a constant, exhausting struggle from the moment I hit first or second grade. I was always, always the kid who was out of his seat. Like, the teacher would be up at the chalkboard explaining fractions or whatever, and I'd be up at the pencil sharpener for the fifth time, or wandering over to look at the class pet, or just standing by my desk because sitting in that hard little plastic chair felt like absolute torture. My body just rejected it. \n\nAnd it wasn't just the moving around, either. I was constantly blurting out answers. If the teacher asked a question and I knew it, I couldn't raise my hand and wait to be called on. I just couldn't physically hold it in. The answer would just shoot out of my mouth before I even realized I was talking. I didn't mean to be disrespectful or disrupt the class, it just... bypassed my brain entirely. \n\nAnd the homework... oh man, my poor mom. It was a total nightmare. I was constantly losing my assignments. She would sit down with me at the kitchen table, we'd spend an hour doing a math worksheet, I'd physically put it into my folder, and somehow by the time I got to school the next morning, it was just gone. Vanished. Sucked into a black hole in my backpack. So, of course, the teachers were always sending notes home. My mom kept a whole file of them, I swear, and it was always the exact same story. They'd write, \"He's a bright boy, he grasps the concepts, he's smart enough to do the work, but he just won't sit still,\" or \"He needs to learn to stay in his seat and stop interrupting.\" \n\nIt used to drive my parents crazy because they knew I wasn't stupid, you know? Like, they knew I was bright enough to get straight A's, but I was getting C's and D's on my report card for \"citizenship\" or \"conduct\" just because I couldn't sit quietly at a desk for six hours a day. So yeah, this definitely isn't some new thing that just popped up as an adult. It's been my whole life, really. Just this motor running inside me that won't ever shut off, ever since I was a little kid.\n\nDoctor: Did your parents or teachers ever take you to see a doctor or a specialist about your restlessness and inability to sit still when you were a child?\n\nPatient: No, actually... no, they never did. Which, you know, looking back on it now with how much of a struggle it was, you'd think someone would have flagged it and said, 'Hey, maybe he needs to see a pediatrician or something.' But my parents... well, my dad was a mechanic, a real old-school, blue-collar guy, and he just had this mindset that I was just a rowdy boy. He'd always say I just had a motor on me and needed to run it off. \n\nAnd the teachers, I mean, they complained constantly, like I said about all those notes my mom kept, but it never really escalated to them suggesting a doctor. It was always framed as a discipline issue, you know? Like, 'he needs to try harder to pay attention,' or 'he needs stricter rules at home.' They just thought I was being difficult on purpose or acting out. \n\nPlus, I mean, this was the early nineties. I feel like back then, at least in my neighborhood, people weren't as quick to take their kids to specialists for that kind of stuff. If you were bouncing off the walls, they just told you to go outside and play until the streetlights came on. So my mom's solution was just trying to tire me out physically. She'd sign me up for every sport she could find—baseball, soccer, whatever—just hoping I'd crash at the end of the day. But the thing is, I never really crashed. I'd come home from a two-hour soccer practice and still be pacing around the living room or doing laps around the coffee table while we watched TV. \n\nSo yeah, no doctors or specialists back then. Just a lot of parent-teacher conferences and... well, a lot of groundings. I spent so much time grounded in my room, which, let me tell you, is absolute torture for a kid who physically cannot sit still. I'd just end up taking apart my alarm clock or bouncing a tennis ball against the wall for hours until my dad would yell up the stairs for me to knock it off. But yeah, no one ever thought to actually take me to a doctor for it.\n\nDoctor: Did you exhibit these restless behaviors before the age of 12?\n\nPatient: Wait, didn't I just... I mean, I know I talk a mile a minute, so maybe I completely buried the lead in all my rambling earlier, but yeah, like I was saying just a couple of minutes ago, absolutely. Way before I was 12. \n\nMy mom and I were just talking about it, and she says I was exactly like this back in grade school, too. I was always the kid who was out of his seat, wandering around the classroom when I was supposed to be doing desk work. And the blurting out answers—that was a huge one, just totally unable to keep my mouth shut and raise my hand when I knew the answer. Plus, you know, constantly losing my homework in my backpack even though my mom and I had just done it at the kitchen table the night before. \n\nShe actually kept all those notes the teachers sent home over the years in this old file folder, and it was always the exact same story from every single teacher—that I was bright enough to do the work and grasped the concepts, but I just couldn't sit still or stay quiet. So, yeah, I definitely exhibited all of this stuff when I was really little. It wasn't just a teenager thing or an adult thing. It was first grade, second grade, all of it. I mean, I could probably call my mom right now and she'd talk your ear off for an hour about how exhausted I made her before I even hit middle school. So, yes, definitely before age 12.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced these restless behaviors in multiple settings, such as at work, at home, and in social situations?\n\nPatient: I mean, I don't really... I'm not sure how to answer that, honestly. Because, well, I don't really break my life down into categories like that, you know? Like work, home, social... it all just kind of bleeds together for me, so I haven't really noticed if it's happening in every single one of those specific places. \n\nLike, at work, at the firehouse, we're always doing something anyway. You're checking the rig, you're cooking dinner for the crew, you're working out, or you're out on a call. It's a 24-hour shift, so there's not a lot of just sitting around to begin with. I mean, sure, sometimes we're in the day room watching a game, and I'm usually the one getting up to check on the food or grabbing people drinks or just kind of standing in the back of the room instead of taking a recliner, but... is that me being restless, or is that just me being a firefighter? I don't really know. It's just how we are. \n\nAnd then at home... I live by myself right now, so it's not like I have a wife or kids pointing out that I'm pacing the floors or whatever. I just do my own thing. I'll be home on my off days and I'll start fixing a leaky faucet, then I'll end up out in the driveway washing my truck, and then I'm reorganizing the garage. I'm always moving, but I don't know if I feel that same trapped, intense need to move like I did when I was a kid forced to sit at a school desk, because nobody's forcing me to sit still now. I just do what I want. \n\nAnd socially... I mean, mostly I just hang out with the guys from the station anyway. We'll go to a buddy's house for a barbecue, and I'm usually the guy manning the grill or playing cornhole or throwing a football around with their kids. I'm not really sitting still there either, but nobody really cares if you're up and about at a cookout, you know? \n\nSo I guess... I just haven't really tracked it like that. I haven't really noticed if it's a specific problem across all those different settings because my life is just kind of built around being active anyway. I don't know if that's what you mean by multiple settings, but yeah, I don't really have a clear-cut yes or no for you on that one.\n\nDoctor: Did you often interrupt others or blurt out answers before they finished speaking when you were a child?\n\nPatient: Oh, man, yeah. I mean, I know I brought up the whole blurting out answers in grade school thing just a couple of minutes ago, so yeah, definitely as a kid. I just couldn't hold it in. But honestly, it never really went away. It's actually a huge issue for me right now, even as an adult, especially at the firehouse. \n\nLike, we'll be sitting around the kitchen table or standing by the rig, and the lieutenant or some of the senior guys will be talking through a tactical plan for a drill. Or maybe they're going over how we're going to approach a specific type of call—like, say, a multi-vehicle pileup on the interstate, which we get a lot of because of the big junction just south of our district. And they'll be right in the middle of explaining the staging, or figuring out who's grabbing the extrication tools and who's pulling the first line, and I just... I cut in. It always makes me look like a jerk, or like I'm a know-it-all who isn't respecting the chain of command, which isn't it at all. I respect those guys to death, I really do. I just get this intense pressure when I know what's coming next, or when I see the solution they're building toward, and I just blurt it out. Like, just yesterday, I was trying to sit through this online safety module for work—which, by the way, they make us do these web-based trainings now instead of the old hands-on stuff, and sitting at a computer desk staring at a screen is just absolute torture for me. Anyway, I was sitting there, and I ended up completely dismantling my clicky pen. Just took the whole thing apart—the spring, the ink cartridge, the little plastic cap—and then put it all back together. \n\nBut I didn't *have* to take the pen apart, you know? It wasn't some \"pen dismantling ritual\" that my brain forced me to do to feel safe. If there had been a paperclip on the desk, I would have bent that out of shape instead. If there was a piece of paper, I probably would have folded it or shredded it into a hundred tiny pieces. My hands just needed to be doing something, literally anything, while the guy on the video droned on about hazardous materials protocols. \n\nSo it's never a specific repetitive behavior that I'm driven to do over and over, and definitely no mental acts or counting or anything like that. It's just... general, chaotic movement, I guess. Whatever is handy, whatever gets me out of the chair, whatever keeps my hands busy. I just want to make sure I'm being clear about that, because it's definitely not some kind of organized compulsion. It's just my body needing to do *something* to stop feeling like it's going to crawl out of its own skin.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience this intense need to move or restlessness when you were a child, before you turned 12?\n\nPatient: Oh, man, yeah. Absolutely. It's funny you ask about that age, because I was actually just talking to my mom about this a few weeks ago, right after that awful meeting with my captain. I was venting to her about how I can't seem to just stand still, and she just kind of laughed and sighed at the same time. \n\nShe says I was exactly like this back in grade school, too. I mean, probably even more obvious back then because I didn't have any kind of adult filter or way to hide it. She told me it was just a constant, exhausting struggle from the moment I hit first or second grade. I was always, always the kid who was out of his seat. Like, the teacher would be up at the chalkboard explaining fractions or whatever, and I'd be up at the pencil sharpener for the fifth time, or wandering over to look at the class pet, or just standing by my desk because sitting in that hard little plastic chair felt like absolute torture. My body just rejected it. \n\nAnd it wasn't just the moving around, either. I was constantly blurting out answers. If the teacher asked a question and I knew it, I couldn't raise my hand and wait to be called on. I just couldn't physically hold it in. The answer would just shoot out of my mouth before I even realized I was talking. I didn't mean to be disrespectful or disrupt the class, it just... bypassed my brain entirely. \n\nAnd the homework... oh man, my poor mom. It was a total nightmare. I was constantly losing my assignments. She would sit down with me at the kitchen table, we'd spend an hour doing a math worksheet, I'd physically put it into my folder, and somehow by the time I got to school the next morning, it was just gone. Vanished. Sucked into a black hole in my backpack. So, of course, the teachers were always sending notes home. My mom kept a whole file of them, I swear, and it was always the exact same story. They'd write, \"He's a bright boy, he grasps the concepts, he's smart enough to do the work, but he just won't sit still,\" or \"He needs to learn to stay in his seat and stop interrupting.\" \n\nIt used to drive my parents crazy because they knew I wasn't stupid, you know? Like, they knew I was bright enough to get straight A's, but I was getting C's and D's on my report card for \"citizenship\" or \"conduct\" just because I couldn't sit quietly at a desk for six hours a day. So yeah, this definitely isn't some new thing that just popped up as an adult. It's been my whole life, really. Just this motor running inside me that won't ever shut off, ever since I was a little kid.\n\nDoctor: Did your parents or teachers ever take you to see a doctor or a specialist about your restlessness and inability to sit still when you were a child?\n\nPatient: No, actually... no, they never did. Which, you know, looking back on it now with how much of a struggle it was, you'd think someone would have flagged it and said, 'Hey, maybe he needs to see a pediatrician or something.' But my parents... well, my dad was a mechanic, a real old-school, blue-collar guy, and he just had this mindset that I was just a rowdy boy. He'd always say I just had a motor on me and needed to run it off. \n\nAnd the teachers, I mean, they complained constantly, like I said about all those notes my mom kept, but it never really escalated to them suggesting a doctor. She'd sign me up for every sport she could find—baseball, soccer, whatever—just hoping I'd crash at the end of the day. But the thing is, I never really crashed. I'd come home from a two-hour soccer practice and still be pacing around the living room or doing laps around the coffee table while we watched TV. \n\nSo yeah, no doctors or specialists back then. I'm not sure how to answer that, honestly. Because, well, I don't really break my life down into categories like that, you know? I haven't really noticed if it's a specific problem across all those different settings because my life is just kind of built around being active anyway. I don't know if that's what you mean by multiple settings, but yeah, I don't really have a clear-cut yes or no for you on that one.\n\nDoctor: Did you often interrupt others or blurt out answers before they finished speaking when you were a child?\n\nPatient: Oh, man, yeah. I mean, I know I brought up the whole blurting out answers in grade school thing just a couple of minutes ago, so yeah, definitely as a kid. I just couldn't hold it in. But honestly, it never really went away. It's actually a huge issue for me right now, even as an adult, especially at the firehouse. \n\nLike, we'll be sitting around the kitchen table or standing by the rig, and the lieutenant or some of the senior guys will be talking through a tactical plan for a drill. I completely interrupt them right in the middle of a sentence because the answer or the next step is already in my head, and it just shoots out of my mouth before I can even hit the brakes. \n\nIt's like my brain is moving five steps ahead—or at least I think it is—and I just physically cannot wait for them to finish getting the words out. And then, you know, a second later I look around the room and realize I just totally stepped on somebody, usually someone with way more time on the job than me, and I completely messed up the flow of the discussion. It always makes me look like a jerk, or like I'm a know-it-all who isn't respecting the chain of command, which isn't it at all. I respect those guys to death, I really do. I just get this intense pressure when I know what's coming next, or when I see the solution they're building toward, and I just blurt it out. It's incredibly frustrating because I'll literally tell myself before a briefing, 'Okay, just listen this time, keep your mouth shut, let the captain speak,' but then someone starts talking and boom, I'm doing it again before I even realize my mouth is open. I’m really trying to think back to when I was little—like, you know, elementary school or junior high—and I honestly just don't know if I can say yes or no to that. She had this whole system, like a chore chart on the side of the fridge, and if you stepped out of line or didn't do your part, you knew exactly what was coming. You were grounded, or you lost TV time, or you were stuck pulling weeds in the backyard all weekend. So I feel like I always kind of knew there was a penalty for messing up, you know? It's just hard for me to look at it as a specific problem across different settings when my entire lifestyle is just built around never really sitting down anyway.
